title: Tracking Serial Criminals with a Road Metric

source.pdf_page_offset_note: PDF and printed page numbers both run from 1 through 19.

context_sources.use: Official COMAP problem summary on page 1 and award designation for control 7273 on page 2.

limitations: Extracted quotation marks contain encoding artifacts, but prose, section boundaries, and numerical content remain readable.
Equations on pages 5, 6, and 9 were checked against full-resolution renders because some mathematical glyphs are degraded in extracted text.
The paper provides no source code, raw event table, geographic coordinates, road graph file, grid resolution, or parameter-selection log.
All 19 pages were visually reviewed through contact sheets; key formula, prediction, and map pages were checked at full resolution.
The context document is a results compilation containing an official problem summary rather than a standalone original problem sheet.

required_deliverables: Develop a method to aid a local police agency investigating serial criminals.
Use at least two different schemes to generate a geographical profile.
Develop a technique that combines the schemes into a useful prediction for law enforcement.
Estimate or guide possible locations of the next crime from times and locations of past crime scenes.
Describe exactly how any additional evidence enters the estimate.
Estimate reliability for a given situation and provide appropriate warnings.
paper_interpretation: A road-distance kernel model predicts the location of a future crime.
A road-metric adaptation of Rossmo's model predicts the offender's residence.
The paper treats the union of all displayed hotspots as its combination strategy.
task_reconstruction.scope_mismatch: The two schemes estimate different target variables, and no mathematical fusion rule converts them into one calibrated next-crime prediction. Reliability is discussed qualitatively rather than estimated for a given case.

section_map.summary: States the road metric, time-dependent KDE, Rossmo residence model, two case studies, and a broad success claim.
Maps the theoretical models, case studies, improvement discussion, conclusion, executive summary, and references.
Defines future-crime and residence targets, previews three modeling stages, and begins scope assumptions.
Limits the method to one automobile-using offender in a compact region and constructs a highway graph.
Defines a grid-based shortest-route distance and substitutes it into a normalized Gaussian-style kernel.
Introduces an empirical increasing bandwidth and begins pointwise weighted linear extrapolation of density fields.
States the weighted normal equations and motivates a road-metric best-fit circle for residence estimation.
Rejects an unstable radial fit and defines a generalized centroid plus mean road-distance radius.
Replaces Euclidean distance with road distance, borrows exponent parameters, and sets the buffer radius to half the fitted radius.
Introduces 20 incidents and displays a highway graph over a qualitative road-distance field.
Uses the first 19 incidents and the known time of incident 20 to predict its location, then begins the residence analysis.
Shows the road-metric circle and Rossmo heatmap and evaluates the known residence by qualitative priority band.
Shows a 3D Rossmo surface and introduces the 22-event Atlanta subset.
Displays road distance and a one-step-ahead heatmap whose held-out crime is outside the dominant hotspot.
Shows the fitted road circle and an in-sample Rossmo heatmap centered near the known residence.
Shows a second 3D surface and proposes terrain and victim-profile extensions.
Acknowledges computational and tuning limits, claims both methods accurate, and begins an operational summary.
States applicability warnings and describes both outputs as prioritized search hotspots rather than absolute probabilities.
Lists geographic profiling, KDE, regression, case-report, and animal-foraging sources.

contributions.summary: Builds a common road-network distance and inserts it into a spatial kernel so highway access shapes the prediction field.
Makes kernel spread increase with elapsed time so recent incidents remain spatially concentrated while older incidents diffuse.
Attempts to extrapolate a future spatial density through pointwise time-weighted least squares.
Replaces an unstable circle fit with a generalized squared-distance center and mean-distance radius under the road metric.
Adapts a buffer-zone residence model to the same road metric used by the next-crime model.
Uses a one-step held-out incident and overlays known residences to make model behavior inspectable on two historical cases.
Translates continuous fields into priority regions and progressive search bands for a law-enforcement audience.

nodes.label: Historical case outcomes and known residences

dependency_graph.missing_edge: No calibrated fusion node combines R1 and R2 into a single prediction with reliability.

assumptions.summary: All incidents in the analyzed series are attributed with high certainty to one individual.
assumptions.consequence: Organized, gang, copycat, and mislinked incidents are excluded.
assumptions.verification: No linkage uncertainty or contamination test is modeled.

assumptions.summary: The offender travels mostly by automobile.
assumptions.consequence: Highway access dominates walking, public transit, and mixed-mode movement.
assumptions.verification: The case data do not independently validate travel mode.

assumptions.summary: Discovery locations approximate crime locations, including treating body dump sites as murder sites.
assumptions.consequence: Transport of victims or delayed discovery can displace the modeled event process.
assumptions.verification: The two case narratives cite supporting evidence but do not model residual location uncertainty.

assumptions.summary: Crimes occur within one city or county; wider series should first be clustered.
assumptions.consequence: The model avoids interstate or international mobility and depends on an unspecified pre-clustering step.

assumptions.summary: Drivers use a shortest route, prefer highways when beneficial, side-street cost is Manhattan distance, and freeway cost is Euclidean edge length.
assumptions.consequence: Speed, directionality, congestion, turn delay, local-road topology, and route heterogeneity are omitted.
assumptions.verification: No observed travel-time or route data calibrate the metric.

assumptions.summary: Older incidents should diffuse more because recent incidents are more predictive.
assumptions.consequence: A fixed increasing bandwidth controls both spatial spread and time weighting.
assumptions.verification: The chosen arctangent bandwidth is described as an empirical good fit without a disclosed loss or validation set.

assumptions.summary: The offender avoids a home buffer while expending roughly comparable travel effort across crimes.
assumptions.consequence: A center and mean radius summarize possibly multimodal or directional offense patterns.
assumptions.verification: No alternative home-anchor mechanism is tested.

assumptions.summary: Attacks and murders in the Sutcliffe series are treated identically.
assumptions.consequence: Victim survival, offense type, target population, and detection process do not affect weights.
assumptions.verification: No event-type sensitivity analysis is reported.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Major highway entrances and exits are manually represented as graph vertices, with intervening road sections as edges weighted by Euclidean length.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: Map source, coordinates, directionality, speed limits, local streets, traffic, and graph-construction reproducibility are absent.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The region is partitioned into an m by n grid and every pairwise cell distance is precomputed and stored.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: Grid extent, cell size, alignment, boundary handling, and discretization error are not reported; storage scales quadratically in the number of cells.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Bandwidth h(t)=2.5 arctan(2t+0.2), with t in weeks, is selected empirically.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: No tuning cases, scoring rule, unit reconciliation, or sensitivity result supports the constants.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Rossmo exponents f=g=1.2 are transferred from a Manhattan-distance model, and the buffer radius is set to half the road-metric mean radius.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: The transferred exponents and half-radius rule are not re-estimated under the new metric.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Nineteen Sutcliffe incidents and the known time of incident 20 are used to predict the held-out location.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: The event-time input would be unknown operationally, and the event table and coordinates are not published.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Twenty-two Atlanta murders described as conclusively linked to Wayne Williams are retained; 21 predict the final location.
data_and_preprocessing.risk: Selection and linkage uncertainty are not propagated, and only one final-event holdout is evaluated.

models.summary: Road distance is the minimum of a Manhattan side-street route and a route entering and leaving a Euclidean-length highway graph.
models.purpose: Represent automobile accessibility more realistically than straight-line distance.
models.algorithm: Dijkstra shortest paths plus grid-to-vertex Manhattan distances.
failure_modes: length called travel time without speeds

models.summary: A road-distance exponential kernel is normalized per incident and averaged, with bandwidth increasing as incident age grows.
models.purpose: Estimate a spatiotemporal field for future incident locations.

models.summary: Density values at each grid cell are linearly extrapolated through time-weighted least squares.
models.purpose: Predict a density field at a future event time.

models.summary: A road-metric Fréchet-style center minimizes squared distance to all incidents and mean distance defines a radius.
models.purpose: Provide a stable center and buffer-scale estimate for residence profiling.

models.summary: Rossmo's buffer-zone scoring formula is rewritten with road distance and normalized over grid cells.

verification.summary: A three-point perturbation example exposes instability in the naive circle objective and motivates a generalized center.
verification.strength: Tests a structural failure mode before choosing the revised estimator.
verification.limitation: The revised estimator's robustness and sampling uncertainty are not quantified.

verification.summary: The first 19 Sutcliffe incidents predict incident 20; the actual cell is reported as 8.58 times the average cell probability.
verification.strength: Separates one target location from the fitting incidents and reports one relative score.
verification.limitation: Uses the target event time, omits baselines and search area, and tests only the last incident.

verification.summary: The known Sutcliffe residence is overlaid on an in-sample residence heatmap and assigned to a second or third priority band.
verification.limitation: No band area, rank, percentile, search-cost curve, or holdout crime subset is reported.

verification.summary: The first 21 Atlanta incidents predict incident 22, which lies away from the dominant hotspot; the result is called a nontrivial probability without a numerical metric.
verification.strength: The paper acknowledges a visibly weaker case instead of hiding it.
verification.limitation: No log score, rank, hit threshold, calibrated probability, or baseline comparison supports the qualitative assessment.

verification.summary: The known Williams residence lies near the dominant in-sample Rossmo hotspot.
verification.limitation: All incident locations inform the surface; there is no out-of-sample residence case or search-efficiency metric.

verification.summary: The paper identifies bandwidth and Rossmo exponents as undertested and proposes later parameter testing.
verification.strength: Names the most consequential tuning gap.
verification.limitation: No sensitivity result or provisional uncertainty bound is supplied in the paper.

results_trace.summary: A road-kernel hotspot contains the held-out Sutcliffe incident and assigns its cell 8.58 times average-cell probability.
results_trace.uncertainty: One case, one final-event holdout, target-time leakage, no baseline, and grid-dependent relative score.

results_trace.summary: The Sutcliffe residence is described as lying in a second or third priority band.
results_trace.uncertainty: No numerical rank, search area, confidence, or independent evaluation.

results_trace.summary: The Atlanta held-out incident lies outside the main predicted hotspot but receives an unspecified nontrivial value.
results_trace.uncertainty: Failure is acknowledged but not scored against baselines or an operational acceptance rule.

results_trace.summary: The Williams residence is near the dominant Rossmo hotspot.
results_trace.uncertainty: Retrospective in-sample overlay with no search-cost curve.

results_trace.summary: The two output fields are combined operationally by advising police to inspect all identified hotspots.
results_trace.uncertainty: This is a union of outputs for different targets, not a fitted or decision-theoretic fusion rule.

results_trace.summary: Applicability is limited to known crime sites, small regions, and automobile travel, and fields are described as relative search priorities rather than absolute probabilities.
results_trace.uncertainty: Warnings are qualitative and no case-specific reliability estimate is produced.

writing_logic.summary: The introduction previews a common distance layer, future-crime density, and residence estimation before the mathematics.
Scope assumptions lead directly into the transportation representation they enable.
A visible failure of the naive circle is shown before the revised definition.
Both case studies repeat map, next-event field, residence field, and assessment subsections, supporting comparison.
The conclusion calls the methods accurate and treats listing all hotspots as synthesis without resolving their different targets or quantifying reliability.
The executive summary is audience-specific and gives limitations before operational search guidance.

language_observations.summary: The abstract names the data, common road metric, two model families, two cases, and intended decision use in a compact sequence.
Strong hotspot is partly supported by an 8.58 relative cell score, but average-square probability depends on the arbitrary grid and does not state search cost.
Very nontrivial probability and reasonably near are used for the visibly weak Atlanta prediction without numerical definitions.
Could very easily locate Williams converts an in-sample visual hotspot into an operational claim without search-area or resource metrics.
Both methods proved accurate overstates evidence from two cases, two final-event checks, and known-residence overlays.
The executive summary usefully distinguishes relative hotspots from absolute probability and states three applicability conditions.

visualization_observations.summary: A compact before-and-after geometry makes instability of the naive circle objective immediately visible.
A road graph is overlaid on a qualitative distance field from the known residence.
visualization_observations.weakness: No coordinates, distance units, numeric colorbar, geographic scale, or local-road layer is shown.

visualization_observations.summary: Training incidents and the held-out target are marked directly on the future-crime heatmap.
visualization_observations.weakness: No axes, numeric colorbar, contours, search-area threshold, or baseline surface is shown.

visualization_observations.summary: The generalized road circle and residence heatmap expose intermediate geometry and the known target location.
visualization_observations.weakness: Priority bands are only color impressions; rank and cumulative search area cannot be read.

visualization_observations.summary: A 3D surface emphasizes multiple Rossmo peaks.
visualization_observations.weakness: Perspective, missing axes, and missing target overlay reduce operational interpretability.

visualization_observations.summary: The Atlanta road field and held-out crime plot reveal that the target is outside the dominant predicted region.
visualization_observations.weakness: The same rainbow-like palette lacks numeric values and no failure threshold is marked.

visualization_observations.summary: The Atlanta road-circle geometry and known residence are overlaid on the residence field.
visualization_observations.weakness: The display gives no out-of-sample status, percentile rank, or cumulative area searched.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Using one domain-specific road metric across multiple models may make a Problem B solution feel coherent and tailored, but award status does not prove this feature caused the result.
alternative_explanations: Clear writing, historical cases, mathematical breadth, or other judging factors may have dominated.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: Showing a failed naive model before a revised estimator may demonstrate mathematical judgment to reviewers, but this remains a cross-paper hypothesis.
alternative_explanations: The revised estimator itself is not fully validated and may not have affected judging.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: An executive summary framed as actionable search guidance may improve stakeholder usefulness, but no official commentary attributes the award to this section.
alternative_explanations: The executive summary may have been a prompt expectation rather than a differentiating strength.

weaknesses.summary: The road metric is described as travel time but uses uncalibrated Manhattan and Euclidean lengths without road speeds, direction, congestion, turn costs, or local-road topology.
Grid resolution and map extent are absent, so discretization error and the quadratic all-pairs storage burden cannot be reproduced.
The bandwidth function and constants are called an empirical good fit without a tuning dataset, scoring rule, sensitivity result, or unit justification.
Pointwise linear extrapolation of densities is not constrained to remain nonnegative or integrate to one.
The refined best-fit circle defines a center and mean radius but does not minimize radial residuals, quantify outlier influence, or report center uncertainty.
Rossmo exponents are transferred from Manhattan distance and the buffer radius is set to half the mean radius without road-metric recalibration.
The held-out prediction uses the known time of the future crime, which would be unavailable in operational deployment; the claimed rapid stabilization is not demonstrated.
The 8.58-times-average-cell score depends on grid size and is not accompanied by hit rate, log score, search-area efficiency, or a baseline.
Residence accuracy is judged by qualitative color bands without rank, percentile, cumulative search area, or a held-out evaluation.
The Atlanta held-out crime misses the dominant hotspot, yet success is defended with undefined phrases rather than a predeclared acceptance criterion.
The known residence is evaluated on a surface fitted with all offense locations, so the result is retrospective and not an independent test.
The paper does not mathematically combine two geographical-profile schemes; it unions hotspots that refer to different targets.
Applicability warnings are useful but no case-specific reliability estimate, calibrated interval, or abstention criterion is provided.
Operational recommendations do not quantify false-positive burden, privacy impact, geographic bias, or the distinction between search priority and evidence of guilt.
Maps and heatmaps lack coordinates, physical scale, numeric colorbars, uncertainty, cumulative search contours, and color-accessible palettes.

independent_extensions.label: Calibrated multimodal travel graph
independent_extensions.proposal: Use directed road edges with travel-time distributions, local streets, turn penalties, time-of-day traffic, barriers, and optional walking or transit layers.
independent_extensions.test: Compare shortest-path times with held-out route observations and report error by region and time of day.

independent_extensions.label: Proper graph spatiotemporal density
independent_extensions.proposal: Use graph heat kernels or constrained nonnegative density evolution with bandwidth and temporal decay chosen by rolling-origin log score.
independent_extensions.test: Verify nonnegativity, normalization, calibration, and performance against uniform, recency, Euclidean KDE, and historical-frequency baselines.

independent_extensions.label: Target-aware scheme fusion
independent_extensions.proposal: Define a joint latent-offender model linking residence, route choice, victim opportunity, and next-event location, or keep separate targets and combine only at the decision layer with an explicit resource-loss function.
independent_extensions.test: Use nested rolling-origin evaluation and compare fusion against each scheme alone under search-area and false-positive costs.

independent_extensions.label: Reliability and abstention layer
independent_extensions.proposal: Estimate calibrated predictive regions, bootstrap sensitivity to incident linkage and coordinates, detect out-of-scope cases, and abstain when calibration or transport assumptions fail.
independent_extensions.test: Measure coverage, expected calibration error, area-at-coverage, and failure detection on perturbed and external series.

independent_extensions.label: Operationally safe geographic profile
independent_extensions.proposal: Present cumulative search-area curves and priority regions as resource-allocation aids, never as guilt scores, and audit geographic and demographic false-positive burdens.
independent_extensions.test: Run blinded analyst studies, privacy review, subgroup/region burden analysis, and counterfactual map perturbations.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Transport-network data require provenance, calibrated edge costs, directionality, resolution, and route validation.
A domain-specific graph metric can unify models only when it preserves units, behavior, and metric assumptions.
Spatiotemporal density evolution must preserve probability constraints and tune bandwidth by rolling-origin validation.
Multiple required schemes need an explicit target-consistent fusion or decision rule rather than side-by-side hotspots.
Keep next-event, offender-residence, and patrol-allocation targets distinct throughout modeling and evaluation.
Use constructed perturbations to expose unstable geometry, then quantify robustness of the replacement estimator.
Use leakage-free rolling-origin spatial backtesting with baselines and operational search metrics.
Reliability must be case-specific, calibrated, assumption-aware, and capable of abstention.
Geospatial fields need coordinates, scale, numeric colorbars, target overlays, uncertainty, and cumulative search contours.
Trace every official clause through scheme, fusion, prediction, extra evidence, reliability, warning, and executive answer.
Spatial success adjectives require predeclared rank, score, coverage, or search-area evidence.
Treat geographic profiles as resource-priority aids, not guilt probabilities, and audit false-positive and privacy harms.
Choose graph-distance algorithms and caching from explicit time-memory-grid tradeoffs rather than storing all cell pairs by default.

unresolved_questions: What original event coordinates, dates, road graph, map projection, and grid resolution generated the figures?
What loss and data were used to select h(t)=2.5 arctan(2t+0.2)?
Does the pointwise weighted extrapolation ever produce negative values or total mass different from one?
How sensitive are hotspots to the unavailable future event time used in both held-out tests?
How do Euclidean KDE, recency-only, uniform, and unmodified Rossmo baselines perform under the same grid?
What numerical fusion rule combines next-crime and residence fields when they represent different target variables?
What search-area percentile contains each held-out crime and each residence?
How should series-linkage uncertainty, dump-site displacement, and non-automobile travel alter reliability?
Can a later Problem B paper supply calibrated uncertainty and decision-safe deployment rules for geographic profiling?
